claims.text: The as-cast high-entropy alloy is in a fully disordered random solid-solution state without significant nanoscale ordering.
The as-cast alloy shows no measurable superconducting transition in the low-temperature test regime.
Controlled thermal annealing induces nanoscale atomic or compositional ordering in the alloy.
Suitable annealing can induce nanoscale ordering without macroscopic phase separation or significant changes in the overall elemental distribution.
Nanoscale ordering or local chemical clustering modifies the local lattice environment.
Thermal annealing reduces excessive atomic disorder and promotes localized ordering.
Localized ordering increases the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
The annealing-induced electronic changes facilitate Cooper-pair formation.
Facilitated Cooper-pair formation leads to the emergence of a superconducting transition.
Annealed samples will exhibit a superconducting transition that is absent from the as-cast samples under identical test conditions.
The predicted transition will be observable through a resistance drop and either a superconducting energy gap or diamagnetic onset.
The mechanism is expected to apply only when annealing produces moderate nanoscale ordering without phase separation or major compositional change.
Departures from the specified structural and processing regime may produce different superconducting behavior.
Prior evidence supports a link between nanoscale ordering and enhanced superconductivity.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome treats a resistance drop together with either a superconducting gap or diamagnetic onset as evidence, whereas the falsification rule uses disjunctive wording under which absence of any one of these signals could falsify the hypothesis even if another superconducting signal is clearly present.
